bibliographic.title: Who judges the judges? Governance from metrics: a runtime framework for continuous LLM compliance monitoring
bibliographic.citation_apa: Dussert, J. (2026). Who judges the judges? Governance from metrics: A runtime framework for continuous LLM compliance monitoring. Preprint. arXiv:2605.24737.

methodology.method_family: framework design and implementation with benchmark evaluation
methodology.study_design: Design, implementation, and evaluation of an open-source runtime governance framework (govllm) validated on a ground-truth corpus of annotated prompt/response pairs using multiple on-premise small language model judges
methodology.sample_description: Ground truth corpus of 49 annotated prompt/response pairs across five regulatory criteria, evaluated by four on-premise small language models (1.7B–7B parameters)
methodology.sector: Regulated environments; EU regulatory and public-sector contexts referenced (EU AI Act, GDPR, ANSSI, accessibility)
methodology.technology_context: govllm open-source runtime framework with governance-driven routing, specialised LLM regulatory judges per criterion, on-premise evaluation, continuous observability, and human arbitration on inter-judge disagreement

eligibility.decision_rationale: The paper directly proposes and evaluates a runtime framework for continuous LLM compliance monitoring, governance-driven routing, regulatory judge panels, human arbitration, and alignment with EU AI Act, GDPR, ANSSI, and accessibility requirements in regulated deployment contexts.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Only partial front-matter and selected page excerpts were supplied; complete methods, full results, and limitations sections may extend beyond the provided text.

appraisal.notes: Strong conceptual and architectural contribution with reported agreement rates and bias analysis, but empirical validation is limited to a small annotated corpus and four on-premise SLMs; some architectural claims are explicitly deferred to future work.

cerqual.explanation: Findings are internally coherent and highly relevant to runtime LLM governance and compliance monitoring, but confidence is moderated by the small benchmark sample, partial text availability, and stated future-work validation for some architectural elements.

coding.theme: Continuous runtime governance and compliance monitoring for deployed LLM systems
coding.subtheme: Regulatory judge panels, uncertainty signaling, and human arbitration
concepts: test → human gate → production → quarantine pipeline
rq_alignment: risk and bias in automated evaluation

synthesis.main_claim: Regulatory compliance for deployed LLM systems should be treated as a continuous, measurable runtime signal derived from observability rather than as a binary, audit-time verdict.
synthesis.contribution: Introduces the governance-from-metrics principle and the open-source govllm framework, including governance-driven routing, specialised regulatory LLM judges, reframing inter-judge disagreement as regulatory uncertainty warranting human arbitration, and empirical validation on a 49-pair ground-truth corpus with four on-premise SLMs.
synthesis.limitations: Empirical validation is based on only 49 annotated prompt/response pairs and four small on-premise models; some architectural elements are described as left for future empirical validation; conversational-system specificity is limited despite interaction-level transparency claims.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as central evidence on runtime LLM governance, continuous compliance monitoring, judge-panel design, human escalation, on-premise evaluation constraints, and EU-regulatory-aligned observability in regulated deployments.

evidence.claim: Paper focuses on continuous runtime LLM compliance monitoring rather than binary audit-time conformity.
evidence.excerpt: Current approaches to AI compliance treat conformity as a binary, audit-time verdict rather than a continuous, measurable property of production systems.

evidence.claim: Proposes governance-from-metrics and the govllm open-source runtime framework.
evidence.excerpt: We introduce governance from metrics, a principle whereby regulatory compliance is derived as a continuous signal from runtime observability rather than from static assessments.

evidence.claim: Uses specialised LLM regulatory judges and treats disagreement as a signal for human arbitration.
evidence.excerpt: a panel of regulatory judges — LLM evaluators specialised per criterion (EU AI Act, GDPR, ANSSI, accessibility) — whose inter-judge disagreement we reframe not as noise but as a regulatory uncertainty signal warranting human arbitration.

evidence.claim: Empirical validation uses a small annotated corpus and four on-premise SLMs.
evidence.excerpt: We validate this approach through a ground truth corpus of 49 annotated prompt/response pairs across five regulatory criteria, evaluated by four small language models (SLMs — 1.7B–7B parameters) running fully on-premise.

evidence.claim: Reports inter-model agreement rates and absence of a single dominant judge.
evidence.excerpt: Agreement rates range from 51.5% (mistral:7b) to 69.1% (phi4-mini), with no single model dominating across all criteria

evidence.claim: Addresses regulated environments and on-premise evaluation as a regulatory requirement.
evidence.excerpt: in regulated environments subject to data sovereignty requirements, routing compliance evaluation through external APIs may itself conflict with the obligations being assessed. On-premise evaluation is therefore a regulatory requirement, not a design preference

evidence.claim: Frames generative AI systems as dynamic and poorly served by point-in-time governance.
evidence.excerpt: agentic and generative AI systems are dynamic by nature — their behaviour evolves with use, context, and model updates. Yet most existing governance approaches remain frozen in point-in-time assessments

evidence.claim: Proposes a governed qualification lifecycle with human gate and drift detection aligned to AI Act art. 9.
evidence.excerpt: we propose a formal test →human gate → production →quarantine pipeline implementing continuous behavioural drift detection aligned with AI Act art. 9 requirements.

evidence.claim: Positions govllm as operational tooling for runtime monitoring aligned with EU AI Act, GDPR, ANSSI, and accessibility.
evidence.excerpt: govllm is designed to bridge this gap — operationalising AI governance in direct alignment with the EU AI Act, the GDPR, ANSSI security requirements, and accessibility standards.

evidence.claim: Operationalises transparency at the interaction level with real-time judge evaluation and surfaced scores.
evidence.excerpt: it operationalises the transparency obligations of EU AI Act article 13 at the interaction level: each model response is evaluated in real time by a judge LLM against a governance profile defined for the active use case, and the resulting scores are surfaced directly to the user

evidence.claim: Some architectural elements are explicitly deferred to future empirical validation.
evidence.excerpt: Inter-judge variance as a regulatory signal, epistemic discrimination across model families, and trajectory-based routing are formalised architecturally in §5 and left for empirical validation in future work (§7).

evidence.claim: Documents judge-specific position bias affecting agreement by up to 25 percentage points.
evidence.excerpt: a judge-specific position bias that degrades agreement by up to 25 percentage points across three question- order conditions (original, reversed, permuted).
